Long-Term Impact of Vutrisiran in Patients With TTR Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy: 1-Year Efficacy and Safety Outcomes From the HELIOS-B Open-Label Extension

Garcia-Pavia P, Witteles R, Morbach C et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: Open-label extension of a randomised controlled trial (HELIOS-B), analysis through month 48.
Key Question: Are the mortality and morbidity benefits of vutrisiran in ATTR-CM sustained long term, and does earlier initiation confer additional advantage?
Key Findings:
  • Continuous vutrisiran versus delayed initiation (placebo/vutrisiran): 37% lower risk of first CV event or all-cause mortality (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.51–0.79) and of all-cause mortality alone (HR 0.63, 0.46–0.84).
  • Better preserved KCCQ-OS (LS mean difference 9.0 points), improved or stable NYHA class (OR 1.6), and lower NT-proBNP and troponin I (fold-change ratios 0.66 and 0.71).
  • No new safety signals; 466 of 478 eligible patients entered the extension.
Clinical Relevance: Supports early diagnosis and treatment of ATTR-CM, relevant to UK referral pathways and commissioning decisions where diagnostic delay is common.
Limitations: Comparison after the double-blind period is non-randomised and open-label, so it is vulnerable to survivor bias and confounding.

Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in Patients With Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease: ISCHEMIA-CKD EXTEND

Bangalore S, Maron DJ, Anthopolos R et al. · 2026 Nov 07
Study Type: Extended long-term follow-up (median 8 years) of a randomised controlled trial (ISCHEMIA-CKD), with Bayesian secondary analyses.
Key Question: Does an initial invasive strategy improve long-term survival compared with initial conservative management in patients with stable coronary disease, moderate-to-severe ischaemia and advanced CKD?
Key Findings:
  • 777 participants (388 invasive, 389 conservative); vital status retained in 95% of survivors; 429 deaths (55%).
  • 8-year all-cause mortality was 57.4% vs 56.8% (adjusted HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87–1.28); cardiovascular mortality was 40.3% vs 38.4% (adjusted HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.84–1.34).
  • Restricted mean survival time difference was −99 days (95% CI −245 to 46) with invasive management; Bayesian analysis showed a 52% posterior probability of at least 1 percentage point higher mortality with invasive management.
Clinical Relevance: Supports a conservative, guideline-directed medical therapy-first approach in advanced CKD with stable coronary disease, reducing the case for routine angiography in this group.
Limitations: Mortality-only extended follow-up, with no long-term data on angina, quality of life or non-fatal events, and limited power to exclude modest benefit or harm.

JAMA Cardiology

Efficacy and Safety of Routine Postdilation in Balloon-Expandable Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation Platform: The DUOTAP Randomized Clinical Trial

Autherith M, Singer K, Hauptmann L et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: Single-centre, single-blinded RCT (n = 148; 1:1 randomisation with sham procedure in controls).
Key Question: Does routine postdilation of a balloon-expandable TAVI valve improve valve geometry and haemodynamics without increasing procedural harm?
Key Findings:
  • Primary endpoint: fluoroscopic THV asymmetry index was 70% lower with postdilation (median 1.2% vs 2.8%; geometric mean ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.18-0.47; P < .001), consistent across subgroups.
  • Postdilation gave larger THV areas on 3-month CT at inflow, midframe and outflow levels, with significantly less HALT and less mild-or-worse PVL, and a higher Doppler Velocity Index (specific rates not given in abstract).
  • No significant difference in procedure-related adverse events (P = .36).
Clinical Relevance: Provides the first randomised evidence supporting routine postdilation for geometric and haemodynamic optimisation in selected balloon-expandable TAVI patients, which may inform UK implant technique, particularly as TAVI expands to lower-risk and younger cohorts.
Limitations: Single-centre, high-volume operators with selected low-risk anatomy (median EuroSCORE-II 2.3%), and the trial was not powered for clinical outcomes (mortality, valve durability, stroke), so benefit rests on surrogate imaging and haemodynamic endpoints.

Circulation

Dapagliflozin for Renal Protection in Heart Transplant Recipients: A Randomized Clinical Trial

Holmen S, Manintveld O, Damman K et al. · 2026 Nov 08
Study Type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (six European centres; n=430 randomised, 424 analysed).
Key Question: Does dapagliflozin 10 mg slow eGFR decline in stable heart transplant recipients (≥1 year post-transplant, eGFR ≥25)?
Key Findings:
  • Primary endpoint (eGFR slope, 2 weeks to 12 months): +2.0 mL/min/1.73 m² with dapagliflozin vs +0.3 with placebo; between-group difference 1.7 (95% CI 0.1–3.3; p=0.03).
  • No unexpected safety signals; adverse event rates, including infections, were similar between arms.
  • Mean baseline eGFR 67 mL/min/1.73 m²; median 7 years post-transplant.
Clinical Relevance: Provides the first randomised evidence supporting SGLT2 inhibitor use for renal protection in heart transplant recipients, relevant to UK transplant follow-up where calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity is a major concern.
Limitations: The between-group difference was small with a lower confidence limit near zero, and 12-month follow-up with a surrogate eGFR endpoint cannot show effects on hard renal or cardiovascular outcomes.

European Heart Journal

Hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: the H-HeFT trial

Køber L, Skak-Hansen KW, Larsen AH et al. · 2026 Nov 04
Study Type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (1:1; n=592; 23 Danish hospitals; mean follow-up 3.7 years)
Key Question: Does adding hydralazine-isosorbide dinitrate (H-ISDN) to contemporary therapy reduce heart failure events or death in HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%)?
Key Findings:
  • Primary composite (HF hospitalisation, urgent IV/metolazone visit, transplant, LVAD, or death) did not differ: 30.6% vs 30.5% (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.67–1.21; P=0.48).
  • All-cause death: 57 vs 72 events (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.51–1.02), a non-significant trend favouring H-ISDN.
  • Worsening HF events were similar: 52 vs 47 patients (HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.68–1.50).
Clinical Relevance: In a predominantly White, older cohort on modern HFrEF therapy, routine add-on H-ISDN is not supported, which is relevant to UK practice where its use is largely confined to ACEi/ARB/ARNI-intolerant patients or self-identified Black patients.
Limitations: Underpowered for the mortality signal, with a low proportion of women (18%) and predominantly White participants limiting generalisability.

Circulation

Statin-Ezetimibe Combination Therapy versus Statin Monotherapy in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of the Randomized Ez-PAVE Trial

Lee SH, Byun YS, Kim JW et al. · 2026 Nov 07
Study Type: Prespecified secondary analysis (second randomisation) of a multicentre RCT (Ez-PAVE; 17 South Korean centres; n=3048; 3-year follow-up).
Key Question: Within a treat-to-target LDL-C strategy, does initial statin-ezetimibe combination therapy improve outcomes compared with statin monotherapy in established ASCVD?
Key Findings:
  • Primary composite (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, revascularisation, unstable angina admission) did not differ: 8.5% vs 7.9% (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.83-1.37; P=0.596).
  • Combination therapy achieved lower median on-treatment LDL-C (intensive arm: 53 vs 62 mg/dL; conventional: 63 vs 70 mg/dL). Ezetimibe was added in 24.8-34.3% of monotherapy patients.
  • Intensive-versus-conventional targeting effect was consistent across regimens (Pinteraction=0.583); safety outcomes were similar.
Clinical Relevance: Supports a pragmatic treat-to-target approach in line with UK lipid pathways, where upfront combination therapy offers faster LDL-C goal attainment but no demonstrated outcome advantage over stepwise ezetimibe addition.
Limitations: Treat-to-target protocol with frequent ezetimibe add-on in the monotherapy arm narrowed between-group LDL-C separation, likely limiting power to detect outcome differences, and findings may not generalise beyond a South Korean population.

JAMA Cardiology

AI-Identified Reasons for Nonescalation of Lipid-Lowering Therapy for Secondary Prevention

Somani S, Kim DD, Ramaraju V et al. · 2026 Nov 07
Study Type: Retrospective cohort study (LLM-based extraction from clinical notes; single integrated US health system)
Key Question: Can LLMs identify treat-to-target use and reasons for lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) nonescalation in ASCVD patients with LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL?
Key Findings:
  • LLM output closely matched clinician annotation (micro-weighted F1 0.80–0.98); of 28,113 ASCVD patients, 13,810 (49.1%) had above-goal LDL-C.
  • A treat-to-target strategy was documented in only 28.1% of notes; LLT was not escalated in 88.7%.
  • Only 40.4% of nonescalation notes gave a reason: patient-reported adverse effects (12.6%), LDL-C near goal (6.9%), patient preference (6.8%), lifestyle preference (6.1%), awaiting repeat bloods (4.6%).
Clinical Relevance: Findings suggest a large secondary prevention treatment gap, broadly relevant to NHS lipid optimisation pathways, though US data limit direct applicability to UK practice (e.g. LDL-C thresholds, inclisiran/PCSK9 access).
Limitations: Reasons were inferred from free-text documentation, which may under-record true clinical decision-making, and no patient outcomes were assessed.

Circulation

Performance of the PREVENT-HF Equations Across Heart Failure Subtypes in Community-Based and Ambulatory Healthcare Samples

Mounsey LA, Wang D, Ribeiro PH et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Retrospective external validation study using five pooled community cohorts and two primary-care EHR samples (US).
Key Question: How well do the PREVENT-HF equations, designed for overall heart failure risk, discriminate and calibrate for 10-year incident HFpEF versus HFrEF?
Key Findings:
  • Discrimination was consistently better for HFpEF than HFrEF: AUROC 0.824 vs 0.789 (pooled cohorts), 0.897 vs 0.833 (BIDMC), 0.864 vs 0.797 (MGB).
  • Average precision/event rate ratios followed the same pattern (e.g. MGB 6.84 vs 4.12).
  • Calibration (ICI) was similar for both subtypes (pooled cohorts: 0.041 vs 0.038).
Clinical Relevance: Supports PREVENT-HF as a usable tool for identifying individuals at risk of either HF subtype, which may inform prevention strategies, though the cohorts are US-based and not validated in UK populations.
Limitations: Subtype-specific risk thresholds were not established, and the equations were not developed for subtype prediction, limiting actionable use.
